title: First on CNN: Whistleblowers tell Democrats documents linked to Trump’s construction projects are being destroyed
content: House Democrats are demanding that the Interior Department retain documents related to President Donald Trump’s construction projects around Washington after whistleblowers warned that key paperwork has already been destroyed before Democrats take power, congressional sources tell CNN. The warnings come as the Trump administration is signaling it will accelerate plans for moving ahead with the projects — a key part of what the president sees as his legacy — to lay as much groundwork as possible before the Democrats take over Congress in January. On Tuesday, the top Democrat in the House Natural Resources committee, which has oversight of the agency that has helped fast-track many of Trump’s projects, plans to issue letters to the Interior Department as well as other federal agencies and private companies, requesting that they “preserve all records and data responsive to oversight” the congressional panel oversees. The targets of the letters from Rep. Jared Huffman, shared first with CNN, give an early indication of what could be in the crosshairs for investigation when the California Democrat becomes chairman of the committee in the new Congress. Multiple credible whistleblowers have approached Huffman’s committee in recent weeks to voice concern that the Interior Department is getting rid of records in anticipation of forthcoming scrutiny, the sources told CNN. The agency oversees much of the national parkland Trump wants to use for his projects. The Interior Department called the whistleblower claims “100% false.” “The Department follows all federal records management obligations as directed by the Department’s ethics officials,” a spokesperson said. Among the other recipients of the preservation letters are the National Park Service and the Bureau of Land Management, which are part of Interior. Letters are also being sent to the Agriculture Department and companies like Lockheed Martin and John Deere that are known to have donated to Trump’s projects. CNN has asked them for comment. Whistleblowers did not say these entities had destroyed documents. However, all letter recipients must reply to certify their compliance, which requires efforts to “preserve existing records collections and productions,” as well as “Identify and recover any deleted information” and “suspend any destruction and deletion practices.” The typically under-the-radar National Resources committee may lack the prominence of the Judiciary or Oversight committees, but in the new Congress it is set to take on the mantle of chief antagonist and auditor of projects that Trump has deeply and personally invested in seeing through. The committee holds legislative jurisdiction over national parks and federal lands, on which Trump is attempting to build projects like the East Potomac golf course and the triumphal arch. “Everything is coming; it’s all coming,” Huffman told CNN in an interview, signaling that his committee is readying a large arsenal of tools that come with the gavel in the new majority. “It’s just going to be an entirely new day,” he said, noting that a win of the magnitude Democrats achieved in the midterms will embolden their investigations, as there is a belief that they have a true mandate from voters who felt the president was focused on the wrong issues. Committee aides expect to hold a high-profile hearing on one or several projects early in the new Congress. The golf course and triumphal arch are chief among the areas of focus. In anticipation of possible obstruction from the administration, the committee is prepared to issue subpoenas. Huffman believes that the committee’s work could stop some of the president’s construction projects from going forward, “especially because we have standing to go to court if we have to,” he said. “We’ll have tools to be able to stop a lot of it.” The committee has also been coordinating with House Oversight and Judiciary, which have mapped out an aggressive approach to investigate other areas of the administration. At the same time, multiple sources close to the approval process on Trump’s projects told CNN they are seeing a new urgency on the part of the administration to get as far as it can by the end of the year. The move to supercharge some of the president’s projects is being met with ire by many in the preservationist community who have been fighting against them. The triumphal arch; a project to put up fencing at Lafayette Square near the White House; the East Potomac Golf Links; and the Tidal Basin Development Concept plan, which includes the president’s Garden of American Heroes, will all see action pushing them ahead over the next 60 days. Some will be going in front of key federal agencies for approval, and others are moving forward in the historical preservation evaluation process. “We’re going to start seeing all of these things happening simultaneously,” said Charles Birnbaum of the Cultural Landscape Foundation. “It is going to be like a storm where it plays out until the new Congress is seated.” The day after the midterm elections, Trump appeared in front of the White House ballroom construction site, signing the last steel beam before it was raised. Davis Ingle, a spokesperson for the White House, said: “President Trump is moving at lightning speed because we don’t have time to waste in our mission to make America greater than ever before.” This story has been updated with additional information.
ranking_reason: House Democrats are demanding that the Interior Department retain documents related to President Donald Trump's construction projects around Washington after whistleblowers warned that key paperwork has already been destroyed before Democrats take power

analysis.reason: House Democrats are demanding that the Interior Department retain documents related to President Donald Trump's construction projects around Washington after whistleblowers warned that key paperwork has already been destroyed before Democrats take power

It provides clear reasons for readers to care, including the potential destruction of documents and the involvement of a sitting president, which has significant public interest.

title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
content:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.
The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.
One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.
Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident.
Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.
It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI).
"Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".
Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.
"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.
He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.
Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.
A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.
No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.
The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".
On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.
In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.
According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".
The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.
"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."
The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.
ranking_reason: Iran's alleged involvement in a terrorist plot at RAF Fairford and other incidents in Europe and the US is a significant political development.

analysis.reason: Iran's alleged involvement in a terrorist plot at RAF Fairford and other incidents in Europe and the US is a significant political development.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant political development, namely the alleged involvement of Iran-backed operatives in a string of terrorist plots in the US and Europe, including the RAF Fairford incident. The article provides evidence-based information and quotes from FBI Director Kash Patel, making it a clear and substantiated report that meets the quality gate criteria.

title: California voters reject one-time wealth tax on billionaires
content: Voters in California have rejected a measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with a net worth of over $1 billion. Proposition 40 became one of the highest-profile and expensive fights over ballot measures this election cycle. With the backing of billionaire funders , groups opposing the proposition spent tens of millions of dollars in ads against the measure. The wealth tax would have applied to around 250 billionaires in California, with the funding raised primarily earmarked for healthcare following federal cuts to Medicaid and other programs. Tech and corporate leaders had threatened to move their residences, and even their businesses, out of California if the measure passed – potentially depriving the state of crucial jobs. The battle over Proposition 40 was one of the most expensive political fights in the country with Google co-founder Sergey Brin funneling just over $100 million to a group trying to defeat the tax. California’s Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom had said he would vote against the measure, instead proposing a national tax on billionaires as he eyes a potential 2028 presidential run. Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, another Democrat, also expressed opposition. But the measure had the backing of other prominent Democrats, including progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Ro Khanna of California, along with several unions. Proponents have said the measure was a necessary response to federal healthcare spending cuts from Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, estimating a shortfall of about $20 billion per year for California moving forward, which threatens the state’s Medi-Cal program that provides healthcare to low-income Californians. They estimated the wealth tax could raise $100 billion, enough to cover the shortfall for about five years. Meanwhile, opponents of the measure had argued it could harm the state where they built their businesses and fortunes, with Brin — who was born in Moscow — comparing the tax in a rare comment to The New York Times to the society he fled as a child and saying he doesn’t want California to adopt socialism. Newsom, in making the case for a national tax, had said Prop 40 would not address other state budget needs like housing, childcare or education and disagreed with “a single advocacy organization” writing “the state’s tax code on its own terms.” Suzanne Jimenez, a sponsor of the measure as part of the group Yes on 40, accused opponents of running a “deeply misleading and corrupt campaign” and criticized the amount of money they poured into it. “Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate,” Jimenez said in a statement , adding, “The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one. This fight to save patient lives and ensure billionaires pay their fair share has only just begun.”
ranking_reason: California voters rejecting a measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with a net worth of over $1 billion

analysis.reason: California voters rejecting a measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with a net worth of over $1 billion

final_quality.reason: This article reports a significant development in the category of people and politics, providing insight into the impact of a proposed tax on billionaires in California. The article provides clear evidence of the measure's potential effects on the state's economy and healthcare system, as well as the opposing views of prominent Democrats and business leaders.
